stem: The magnification factor (MF) is calculated as
options: image size divided by object size
object size divided by image size
explanation: MF = image size ÷ object size; it can also be found as SID ÷ SOD.

stem: A structure measures 15.2 cm on the image, and the magnification factor is 1.3. Its actual size is about
explanation: Object size = image size ÷ MF = 15.2 ÷ 1.3 ≈ 11.7 cm.

stem: An image is made at 40 in SID with an 8-in OID. The magnification factor is
explanation: SOD = 40 − 8 = 32 in, and MF = SID ÷ SOD = 40 ÷ 32 = 1.25.

stem: Linearity testing requires that output in mR/mAs be consistent across mA stations to within
explanation: Linearity tests x-ray output with increasing mAs; mR/mAs must agree to within 10%.

stem: Tested with an electronic kV meter, the kilovoltage should be accurate to within
explanation: Standards call for kV accuracy within ±4 kV of the setting.

stem: Reproducibility testing requires that radiation output stay consistent to within
explanation: Repeated exposures at the same technique must agree to within ±5%.

stem: Collimator accuracy on radiographic equipment should be inspected and verified
explanation: Collimators are checked twice a year, and must be accurate to within 2% of the SID.

stem: The input phosphor of an image intensifier is usually made of
explanation: Cesium iodide absorbs the remnant x-rays efficiently and emits many light photons for each one absorbed.

stem: The gain in brightness that results from the output phosphor being much smaller than the input phosphor is called
explanation: Concentrating the electron image onto a small output phosphor makes it brighter: minification gain.

stem: The total brightness gain of an image intensifier is
options: minification gain multiplied by flux gain
flux gain divided by minification gain
the kVp multiplied by the mA
explanation: Brightness gain is the product of minification gain and flux gain.

stem: Switching an image intensifier to magnification mode
options: has no effect on patient dose
increases patient dose, because the mA is raised automatically
explanation: Less minification makes the image dimmer, so the mA rises to compensate, and entrance skin exposure can increase sharply.

stem: In magnification mode, the electron focal point inside the image intensifier moves
explanation: Higher voltage on the focusing lenses moves the focal point farther from the output phosphor, so the output image is magnified.

stem: Moving the image intensifier closer to the patient during fluoroscopy
explanation: More photons reach the input phosphor, so the automatic brightness control lowers the mA; the shorter OID also reduces magnification.

stem: The automatic brightness control (ABC) in fluoroscopy
options: keeps image brightness constant by adjusting the exposure factors
explanation: As patient thickness changes, the ABC adjusts the mA (and kVp) so the image brightness stays the same.

stem: Spatial resolution is measured in
explanation: Spatial resolution is expressed in line pairs per millimeter (lp/mm), or by the line-spread or modulation transfer function.

stem: Which is desirable in a medical image?
explanation: Noise impairs the image, so a high SNR (more signal, less noise) is desirable.

stem: In digital imaging, a histogram illustrates the
explanation: The histogram plots how many pixels have each value; the system compares it with a default histogram for each body part.

stem: Selecting the wrong body part on a digital system before processing can cause
options: incorrect histogram analysis and a poorly displayed image
explanation: Each body part has its own default histogram; the wrong one makes the computer rescale the image incorrectly.

stem: In computed radiography, an aliasing (moiré) artifact can occur when
options: the anode heel effect is strong
a stationary grid's strip frequency matches the reader's scanning pattern
a focused grid is upside down
explanation: Wavy lines appear when the grid's lead-strip pattern lines up with the sampling pattern of the reader.

stem: Grid frequency is the
options: height of the strips divided by the interspace
kVp the grid is used with
number of lead strips per inch (or per centimeter)
explanation: Grid frequency counts the lead strips per inch or centimeter; grid ratio is strip height divided by interspace width.

stem: The focusing distance (grid radius) of a focused grid is
options: the range of SIDs at which the grid can be used
the height of the lead strips
the number of strips per inch
explanation: A focused grid works only within a range of distances, where its angled strips line up with the divergent beam.

stem: With a linear focused grid, centering the central ray off-center lengthwise, along the strips, causes
explanation: Off-centering along the strips causes no cutoff; off-centering side to side makes the strips no longer match the beam and causes a loss of exposure.

stem: With a linear grid, the central ray can be angled without cutoff
options: along the length of the lead strips
explanation: Angling in the direction of the strips keeps the beam parallel to them; angling across them causes cutoff.

stem: An air gap between the part and the image receptor
options: acts like a grid, because much of the scatter misses the IR
explanation: Diverging scatter leaving the body often bypasses the receptor across the gap, an effect similar to a grid.

stem: A chest radiograph with a 6-in air gap is usually made at what SID, to offset magnification?
explanation: The longer 10-ft SID reduces the magnification that the air gap's added OID would cause.

stem: A moving grid (Potter-Bucky diaphragm) that travels in an almost circular path is described as
explanation: Moving grids may be reciprocating (equal strokes back and forth), oscillating (almost circular) or catapult (rapid forward, slow return).

stem: A compensating (wedge or trough) filter is used to
options: even out receptor exposure across a part of unequal thickness
explanation: The filter is thicker over the thinner part of the body, such as the toes of the foot, giving uniform exposure.

stem: As an x-ray tube ages, vaporized tungsten is deposited on the port window and
options: acts as a filter, decreasing tube output
explanation: The tungsten coating adds filtration, so less radiation leaves the tube.

stem: Using AEC with a field much larger than the part can cause
options: premature termination of the exposure and an underexposed image
explanation: Excess scatter from the body or tabletop reaches the chamber, which ends the exposure too soon.

stem: If the exposure needed is shorter than the AEC's minimum response time, the image will be
explanation: The AEC cannot end the exposure faster than its minimum response time, so a part needing less exposure is overexposed, for example with very high mA.

stem: Which factors influence the half-value layer of an x-ray beam?
options: kV, total filtration and the type of rectification
focal spot size and grid ratio
explanation: Beam quality, and so the HVL, depends on kV, filtration and rectification; mAs changes only the quantity of photons.

stem: In the CR reader, the latent image stored on the photostimulable phosphor plate is released by
explanation: The laser stimulates the phosphor to give off the stored energy as light, which is collected and digitized.

stem: Applying a large exposure to a cold anode can cause
explanation: Sudden heating of a cold anode can crack it; warming the tube up first prevents this.

stem: Which combination produces 20 mAs?
explanation: mAs = mA × time: 200 × 0.1 = 20. The others give 10, 100 and 10 mAs.

stem: To double the exposure reaching the image receptor without changing kVp, the mAs should be
explanation: Receptor exposure is directly proportional to mAs.

stem: Changing the SID from 40 in to 72 in requires the mAs to be multiplied by about
explanation: By the direct square law, (72 ÷ 40)² = 1.8² ≈ 3.24.

stem: Raising the kVp, with all else unchanged, generally
options: increases the share of scattered radiation
explanation: Higher-energy photons undergo more Compton scatter relative to photoelectric absorption.

stem: Which situation produces the most scattered radiation?
options: A small field on a thin part
A large field on a thick part
explanation: Scatter increases with the volume of tissue irradiated: large fields and thick parts.

stem: Geometric unsharpness (penumbra) increases with
explanation: A large focal spot, a long OID and a short SID all widen the penumbra.

stem: Angling the central ray along the long axis of a part produces
explanation: Angling the tube elongates the part's image; tilting the part away from the IR foreshortens it.

stem: Foreshortening of a part on the image occurs when the
options: part is not parallel to the IR
tube is angled along the part
explanation: A part tilted relative to the IR is projected shorter than it really is.

stem: Widening the window width on a digital display
explanation: A wider window spreads more gray values across the display, giving lower contrast; window level controls brightness.

stem: As the bit depth of a digital system increases, it can display
explanation: Gray-scale range is measured in bits; the greater the number of bits, the more shades of gray.

stem: In a flat-panel detector, the signal for each pixel is collected by a
options: detector element (DEL) with a thin-film transistor
explanation: Each detector element has its own thin-film transistor that sends its charge to be read out.

stem: A charge-coupled device (CCD) converts
options: an electric signal into film density
explanation: CCDs read the light from a scintillator or output phosphor and turn it into an electric signal.

stem: Compared with a low-ratio grid, a high-ratio grid
options: requires more accurate centering and leveling
explanation: Taller strips cut off the beam more easily, so centering, leveling and distance must be more exact.

stem: A parallel (nonfocused) grid used at a short SID causes
explanation: Divergent rays at the edges strike the parallel strips at an angle and are absorbed.

stem: A reciprocating (moving) grid is used to
options: remove more scatter than a stationary grid
blur the grid lines so they do not show on the image
explanation: Moving the grid during the exposure blurs out the lead-strip lines.

stem: The lead foil on the back of an image receptor prevents
explanation: Radiation scattered back from the table or wall behind the receptor is absorbed by the lead backing.

stem: Barium and iodine contrast agents absorb more x-rays than soft tissue, so they appear
explanation: Their high atomic numbers make them radiopaque, so the structures they fill appear light.
